In this commentary I explore the significance of Valerie Walkerdine's paper ‘Video Replay: Families, Films and Fantasy’. I review its impact in 1986 and then discuss how some of its ideas about subjectivity and popular culture - specifically film - can be developed in the contemporary context. A recurring fantasy of Rocky II and its reception is that of social and psychological transformation. I address this theme by drawing on the work of Christopher Bollas to argue that Walkerdine's psychosocial analysis continues to facilitate, across a range of contexts, some of the transformational processes described in her article.

Tony Gatlif's 1997 film, Gadjo dilo, portraying the search of a young Frenchman, Stéphane, for an old Gypsy singer, Nora Luca, was heavily criticized by Roma activists for denigrating the image of the Roma through harmful stereotypes and misrepresentations. In this paper, I argue that a Lacanian understanding of the voice as objet a, as it has recently been developed through the work of Mladen Dolar, provides us with a radically different interpretation of the film. Through tracing the object of Stéphane's quest, the acousmatic voice of Nora Luca, I show how Gadjo dilo undermines the notion of authenticity and truth that supports the very idea of true images or unified cultural identities.

Barnaby Barratt  

In a 2008 lecture, Peter McLaren, influenced, I believe, by the writings of Richard Kearney (1998), suggested that the Western tradition has become excessively enchanted with the spiritual-existential question, Who am I? This preoccupation tends to divert us from questions that are more pertinent from the standpoint of immediate political relevance: Where am I? Where are we? Such questions - instigating our reflection on, as well as interrogation and assessment of, our positioning within the nexus of interpersonal, cultural and economic relations - lead us more immediately toward considerations of praxis. How we think about our location within the hierarchies of power and social exploitation, as well as our connectedness with the values of our community, has inspired the emergence of liberation psychologies over recent decades; it is surely also central to any concern with the application of psychoanalytic insights to the mandate of progressive social change.

As is now well known, liberation psychology is the rallying cry of the late Ignacio Martín-Baró (1994), who was murdered by the Salvadoran army in 1989 and who had vehemently advanced a new role for psychologists during the civil wars in Central America (see Hollander, 1997). His ideas drew from many sources, including the work of Albert Memmi, Frantz Fanon, Paolo Freire, and the Latin American freedom and justice movement in Catholic theology. Liberation psychology has definitions both narrow and broad. The narrow definition is that “psychology of liberation is the practice of psychology under the conditions of state repression” (Alschuler, 2006, p. 3). The broader vision is that psychologies of liberation are, as Watkins and Schulman point out, “compass points or orientations in the form of ideas, practices, and projects that nurture an imagination of alternative ways of thinking and acting together that can transform participation in social, economic, and ecological change and address psychological sufferings” (p. 3). The leading figures in this movement are mostly from the “third-world.” They include such eminent writers as Albert Memmi, Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Paolo Freire, Gloria Anzaldúa, Aurora Morales, Susan Griffin, Chela Sandoval, Elizabeth Lira, Enrique Dussel, William Du Bois, James Cone, and Audre Lorde (this list is far from exhaustive).

Social defense theory is used to explore the nature of anxiety and defense in sustainability initiatives. Taking seriously the suggestion that people use social institutions for both creative and defensive purposes, I examine how the organisational processes of a consortium case study seemed to be mobilised to cope with anxiety. The insights contained herein are useful if those working in that domain are to guard against the very wastefulness they ostensibly seek to redress. The data that inform the discussion come from a qualitative research project that sought to explore the psychodynamics of partnering for sustainability.

This is an intriguing book. Diamond and Allcorn have constructed a view of organizations and organizational actors that moves beyond the structural or functional approach. They look inside not only the organization but also the metaphorical selves that inform the reality of organizational operation; and, in so doing, they shed fascinating light on both the ability of organizations to function and their all too frequent moments of dysfunction. Diamond and Allcorn look at organizations that reflect “dis-ease,” that are not “well,” where individuals, groups and units within organizations work at cross-purposes and as a consequence impair the ability of the organization to operate in whatever environment or marketplace it inhabits. The authors approach this clinical task of disentangling sick organizations with a unique and penetrating use of contemporary psychoanalytic theory.

Diamond and Allcorn examine that aspect of human experience which Michel Foucault called “unreason“; they argue that it is not technical “rationality” that holds the key to understanding how to fix injured organizations, but a grasp and knowledge of both the theory and the practices of psychoanalytic observation. Theirs is an implicit argument against the Weberian notion that rationality defines bureaucratic operation. Diamond and Allcorn make clear that, although the organizations examined in their complex and informative case studies are built on “bureaucracies,” to approach an organization only from the standpoint of functional rationality and fixing bits and pieces of “function” ignores key psychodynamic factors that motivate actors. It is not the surface structures of “reason” (however the organization defines them) that hold the keys to a healthier organizational environment. Rather, the consultant's task is to unearth and make visible the complex undercurrents of the “nonrational” (unreason) as it works its way through the organization in unconscious phantasies, in psychological operations like splitting, regression (”childlike behavior amongst participants” (p. 8)) and transference. These kinds of psychological operations lead to organizational chaos and fragmentation.

Mark Edmundson's The Death of Sigmund Freud: The Legacy of His Last Days places Freud's work, often criticized without an appreciation of context, in a rich personal and historical milieu. Edmundson provocatively juxtaposes Freud's deteriorating health with the rise to power of Adolf Hitler (including the occupation and pillaging of Freud's native Austria) and offers not only a psychoanalytic interpretation but also an interpretation of the development of psychoanalysis.

Using Freud's writings on authority as a guide, Edmundson paints Hitler as the prototypical patriarchal figure of authority that, though infantile and fleeting, satisfies the most basic of human needs.

This paper draws on data collected from my recent exploration of how teachers become competent in the area of relationships. In an interview, a student teacher, Kristin, voiced the challenges she faced: ‘I think it is easy enough to get the knowledge the student needs. The problem is, in a way, when people are involved'’. This paper presents an encounter between Kristin and a student after Kristin had started to work as a teacher. It shows the difficulty of being professional when ‘people are involved’, that is, when emotions are at work.

In this essay I describe a process of moving from object relating to object usage in my Comparative Literature course on Literature and Psychoanalysis. My focus is on the iteration of the course that I taught in the fall of 2007, but I also make reference to other versions of the seminar, or, rather, to my sense of the trajectory of my relationship to students' reactions to its material. Carolyn Betensky

Carolyn Betensky

Kingston, Rhode Island, USA

Carolyn Betensky  

Herman Westerink, a professor of Practical Theology and Psychology of Religion at the Protestant Theological Faculty in Vienna, has written a provocative study on the role of guilt in Freud's work. While few with even a glancing familiarity with Freud would be surprised at Westerink's contention that the sense of guilt is central to Freud's thinking, A Dark Trace argues that we have scarcely recognized how central it is. Westerink maintains that Freud's abiding and fervent interest in guilt spanned his entire career, not only the later work, and motivated some of his most perplexing theoretical gambits. Because the sense of guilt has not received its due in scholarly or clinical assessments of Freud's contributions, Westerink suggests, certain Freudian insights and principles - most notably, the Oedipus complex - have been given disproportionate weight, with the result that Freud appears to be more of a systematizer than he ever was. The debates in which Freud engaged with such of his former followers as Rank, Jung and Klein were to some degree related to their different conceptions of the nature and origin of the sense of guilt. Westerink resituates Freud's thinking in the context of a broad swath of intellectual conversations that were taking place in nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Europe, conversations dominated by questions of guilt, morality, conscience and punishment. Recovering a Freud responsive to poets, playwrights, novelists, anthropologists, theologians, and philosophers, as well as one who contrived to guard and stretch his thinking to protect it from the encroaching theories of rival psychoanalysts, Westerink challenges us to read Freud afresh, instead of merely rereading him.

A Dark Trace doubles as an intellectual biography of Freud. Westerink charts Freud's development as a thinker by putting close readings of his texts back in dialogue with their cultural and historical contexts, beginning with his earliest days as a researcher in Vienna. Even before he began his work with hysterics under Charcot in Paris, Freud was thinking along the lines that would later characterize his writing about the relationship between repression and the sense of guilt, as evidenced by a letter he wrote to Martha Bernays in 1883 about a performance he attended of Bizet's Carmen. According to Westerink, who views Freud's musings on the opera as an early case study, Freud was taken by both its plot and the response of its audiences. Already noting a correlation between the “refinements” of the bourgeoisie and their loss of spontaneity and pleasure, Freud was contesting the notion that it is primarily pleasure that humans pursue; even this early in his career, the avoidance of displeasure seemed to him a much more apt mechanism to explain human behavior.

catastrophic experience; symbol formation; difficulties with learning; psychoanalysis and education; social exclusion; parasitic relationship

The paper discusses how social exclusion imposes a parasitic container-contained relationship and, consequently, a catastrophic experience on the subjects. Children who come from backgrounds of social exclusion and who were designated by their teachers as having difficulties learning and as making the teachers feel less than competent were observed at a school in Brazil. The children met with the researcher (the author) once a week, during which time they could play, read, draw, or just talk. Material is presented to show that catastrophe obstructs growth through the use of mechanisms that make contact between container and contained (or vice-versa) unviable. The path from the paranoid-schizoid position to the depressive position is thus blocked, and, as a result, there tends to be difficulty in developing the capacity for symbol formation and then to learn how to read and write and to ‘think thoughts’.

Bosnia; ethnic conflict; identity politics; ego ideal; projective identification

The Dayton Peace Accords set out to protect the three dominant ethnic groups in Bosnia in the aftermath of the 1993-1995 War. However, the peace treaty inscribed ethnic groupings into the constitution as permanent identity constellations. Fifteen years after the cessation of military hostilities Bosnia continues to struggle with the identity limitations imposed on it by the peace treaty. Without the flexibility to create new identity frames, Bosnia remains locked in the identity terms of the conflict. The misrecognition of the nature of identity and particularly the defensive quality by which collective identity frames can protect against threat inhibit a working through of conflicts. A re-evaluation of identity narratives in the context in which they are expressed reveals the defensive purpose they serve. This article explores the problems of accepting at face value the narratives of collectivities under threat and suggests how recognition of the fluid quality of identity may require different strategies by third parties intervening into conflicts.

religious socialization; processes of renunciation; symbolization of experience; cliché; desensualization

The article illustrates Alfred Lorenzer's theory of socialization and symbolization and its usefulness for understanding the psycho-societal emergence of meaning. Using the example of Christian evangelicalism, the article describes the process by which experiences, events, and interactions are symbolized. In this specific case, a rigidified form of symbolization, with its ensuing ideological effects, strips meaning of its playful, tentative qualities and turns it into a dogma or compulsive force. Following Lorenzer, it is argued that this process calls on a ‘clichéd’ structure of ‘authentic’ and ‘secure’ identities.

Frann Michel  

Drawing on research done in the 1960s, Esther Newton (1972) describes professional drag queens as “professional homosexuals“: “the persons who most visibly and flagrantly embody the stigma. … men who dress and act ‘like women’” (p. 3). They are thus at the “opposite pole” from the “ ‘masculine,’ ‘respectable’ homosexuals, [who are] engaged in proving … that persons in the stigmatized category can be just as normal and competent as heterosexuals, ‘… nice persons like ourselves’”(p. 3). But by the early twenty-first century, an audience member at a drag club says, “If you watch the show … you realize they're normal people that work … and love, and do the same things that you do, it's just that they have a little bit different way of expressing their sexuality.” How drag queens came to be seen as “normal people” “like ourselves” is the story of the mainstreaming of queer culture; one strand of that narrative concerns how the productions and representations of queerness serve the needs of a dominantly heterosexual culture. More particularly, how the “professional homosexuals” of the USA's oldest running drag club serve the psychological and social needs of their (predominantly straight) audience is the story of Queens of Heart: Community Therapists in Drag.

To be sure, this documentary about Darcelle XV in Portland, Oregon, offers its psychoanalysis of the audience playfully. (I must disclose that I know the director and assisted with her commentary on the DVD). A note at the beginning of the movie warns us that it “contains clinical terms that may be offensive to some viewers. Any relationship between diagnostic terms and actual audience members or groups is mostly accidental. For a real diagnosis, consult your personal physician.” But this attention to audience, reversing the approach of many other documentaries on drag asks not so much why the performers do drag as why people (and particularly why straight people) like to watch drag. This is not a complete answer to bell hooks's (1992) critique of the voyeurism of a film like Paris is Burning, since - although the club's performers are black, Latino, and Pacific Islander, as well as white, and the audience is apparently all white - race is not explicitly addressed as an issue. Still, the focus on audience helps emphasize that camp drag performance at Darcelle's is skilled, therapeutic labor. The film mixes footage of the performance and the audience with interviews and backstage moments. Title cards using Rorschach inkblots introduce five sections of the movie: “Hysteria,” “Castration Anxiety,” “Gender Complexes,” “Family Dynamics,” and “The Talking Cure.

Lorenzer; depth-hermeneutic method; audience research; affective television; transformation in gender roles

In this interview, Ulrike Prokop, a leading figure in the depth-hermeneutic tradition, reflects on over 30 years, audience research. She discusses, in particular, her more recent work exploring audiences' responses to so-called affective television, including such shows as Supernanny and Germany's Next Top Model. The method she and her colleagues have developed encourages participants to record the associations that occur to them while viewing and to explore these in group discussions. Prokop argues that the method reveals the collective dimensions of audiences' pre- and unconscious responses to these programmes and the impact of social change on their subjective experience.

Walkerdine's ‘Video Replay’ paper analysing a working-class family's reactions to watching a video of Rocky II was pathbreaking: it underlined power relations implicit in participant observation, challenged the differential between ‘high’ and ‘low’ culture and developed a framework for understanding viewers' engagement with film. The paper also makes a transcript of the video-viewing available for subsequent analysis. This commentary rereads the transcript in the light of the contemporary context and my affective responses to the material. The reading draws attention to identifications at play among family members, film characters and researcher, as well as to the ways this family's establishing a harmonious domestic scene allowed violent material to be viewed in relative safety. Fantasy is perceived as having constitutive effects. This reading moderates some of the deterministic implications of focusing primarily on signification.

She is in the process of writing a book drawing on Wilfred Bion's theorisation of knowing, thinking and emotional experience. ‘Mothers’ Knowing/Knowing Mothers' is based on research data from women as they become mothers for the first time. Lorenzer; scenic understanding; interaction forms; psychosocial method; experience-near; symbolization

In this paper two researchers who position themselves within an emergent psychosocial current in the UK apply the concept of scenic understanding to a segment of film footage of an interaction (part of an empirical qualitative research project) to explore what Alfred Lorenzer's theory can add to our existing methodological resources. The film footage shows the creation of a poem by Darren, a 16-year-old offender, and Bob, a local poet employed in a project investigating the rehabilitative potential of one-to-one creative writing sessions. The authors contrast the transcript of this encounter with a ‘scenic composition’, a device they developed to communicate to a research readership the scenic experience of watching a filmed interaction. This contrast forms the basis for bringing together a series of post-Kleinian ideas about modes of knowing (syncretistic perception, reverie, transitional space) with Lorenzer's scenic understanding. Using the idea of provocations in the text, the authors focus on the researcher's emotional experience to explore the psychosocial character of the meanings that emerge concerning Darren's claim, ‘I'm not clever', and how these meanings are communicated amongst Darren, Bob and the researcher. Through the lens of symbolised and unsymbolised emotional experience, play and triangular space, the authors consider Darren's ambivalent relationship to the creative writing activity and conclude with a short discussion of the conceptualisation of unconscious processes suitable to a psychosocial data analytic methodology.

In this article I illustrate the central role of dynamic conflict in the identity changes involved in becoming a mother for the first time. I look in depth at two salient themes in Justine's case: the conflicts between mothering and work and those surrounding separation with her daughter. My analysis of this single case is psycho-social; that is, without reducing to either social or psychological explanations, I attempt to articulate the connections among them. The analysis is informed by a psychoanalytic account of conflict-based unconscious intersubjectivity as a foundation for self-formation and demonstrates how these dynamics work across generations to shape a woman's identity as she becomes a mother. I briefly contrast the mother's experience with the father's. Methodologically, I pay attention to the workings of transference dynamics in the interpretation of empirical interview-based data.

This paper shows, through exploration of interview transcripts, how conceptual elements derived from Lacanian theory can be used for analytic purposes. Rather than colonizing the text with psychoanalytic discourse, it organizes 21 aspects of Lacan's approach to discourse into seven clusters of analytic concepts concerned with the formal qualities of text, the anchoring of representation, the question of agency and determination, the role of knowledge in a text, positions in language, deadlocks of perspective, and the interpretation of textual material. This reading does not claim to unlock the secrets of the text or of those represented in it, nor does it attempt to show how psychoanalysis can be ‘applied’ outside the clinical setting. Instead, through attention to the productive effects of discourse and psychoanalysis, it aims to redeem the promise of those nonreductionist traditions in psychosocial research that attend to the construction of subjectivity.

This article aims to introduce an Anglophone audience to the work of Alfred Lorenzer. It has three main components: it outlines some of Lorenzer's central concepts (the scenic, interaction forms, engrams, symbolisation and desymoblisation, language games and scenic understanding); explores the dialectical relations through which, for Lorenzer, unconscious, bodily and social processes are mutually constituted; and sketches some of the principles informing the depth-hermeneutic method, the tradition of social, cultural and social psychological research to which his ideas gave rise. Throughout, Lorenzer is viewed as seeking to put psychoanalysis on a materialist footing and concerned to assert its critical potential.

As well as supplying biographical details, this short Introduction to the special issue on Lorenzer's work sketches the nature of his debt to Frankfurt School critical theory, highlights his attempt to place psychoanalysis on a materialist footing, and provides an overview of the issue's contents.

Lorenzer; scenic understanding; countertransference; depth-hermeneutic method; social research; drug addiction

This article explores Alfred Lorenzer's notion of scenic understanding through a conflict that beset a data-interpretation panel, part of a study evaluating a programme of psychodynamic therapy for drug-addicted young people. A second interpretation panel, formed in the wake of the first group's collapse, came to understand this conflict as a ‘counter-transference’ to the latent meaning present in the case on which the first panel had been working. This insight, in turn, gave rise to a new understanding of the case itself, in particular the possibility that the interviewee had made less progress in her therapy than appeared to be so.

The role of development worker is a highly political one, and the research on which this article is based explored how such workers negotiated some of the ethical challenges of the job. The research adopted a methodology that, whilst psychoanalytically inspired, was also congruent with the democratic values and experiences of those who were being researched. The authors argue that the validity of the psycho-social method to some extent hangs on the capacity of the researcher to share his or her thinking with the interviewees and involve them in a joint process of sense-making. This is an important methodological innovation given that psycho-social approaches are sometimes criticised for being top-down.

Psychiatrists and psychoanalytic discourse played a significant role in generating the ethnic conflicts that ignited the Balkan war of the 1990s. Interpreted and politicized by Serb psychiatrist/politicians Drs. Jovan Rašković and Radovan Karadžić, the Balkan Oedipus became a totalizing social theory for post-socialist subjectivity. Rašković's (1990) book Luda Zemlja [A Mad Country] provided psychoanalytic justification for ethnic separation and advocated Serb ‘irrational delirium’ as a liberating political force. Radovan Karadžić became notorious as the architect of the Bosnian genocide. The discursive construction of Balkan identity made the region particularly vulnerable to the ethno-analysis promulgated by those two psychiatrists.

Bisexuality is arguably Freud's most overdetermined foundational concept and also the one that has received the least critical attention. The author employs the Lacanian notion of primacy of the signifier to critique psychoanalytic representations of bisexuality as a primordial, undifferentiated state; she suggests that what is in fact primordial and undifferentiated is the signifier itself. Insights from the history of science and feminist theory are used in critically examining the primordial signifier of bisexuality. The author likewise raises the question of the psychoanalytic community's motivations for retaining this signifier.
